records.sourceFile: Prevalence, mechanisms, and return to sport after isolated popliteus injuries in athletes - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Morrissey CD, Knapik DM. Prevalence, Mechanisms, and Return to Sport After Isolated Popliteus Injuries in Athletes: A Systematic Review. Orthop J Sports Med. 2022;10(2):23259671211073617.
paper.abstract: Systematic review, following PRISMA and registered with PROSPERO, of published studies from January 1988 to August 2021 on athletes with isolated popliteus injuries sustained during sport. It describes mechanisms, sports, tear characteristics, treatment, outcomes and return to sport.
paper.tldr: Isolated popliteus injury is rarely reported in athletes and is described only in case reports and small series, here 27 athletes from 19 studies. Most had a traumatic or contact mechanism and a lateral condyle avulsion, and the 13 athletes whose return was reported went back to sport at a mean of about 11 weeks.
paper.methods: Seven databases (PubMed, OVID, MEDLINE, Biosis Previews, SPORTDiscus, PEDRO and EMBASE) were searched for English-language studies of athletes with isolated popliteus injuries sustained in competitive sport, with two reviewers screening independently. Studies with associated posterolateral corner, cruciate or meniscal injury were excluded, and the data were summarised descriptively because the reporting was too heterogeneous for statistical analysis.
paper.findings: Mechanisms were traumatic or contact in 67% (18 of 27), noncontact in 15% (4), and unreported in 19% (5). Avulsions off the lateral femoral condyle occurred in 67% (18) and 85% (23) had swelling; 52% (14) were managed non-operatively and 48% (13) operatively, and complications were reported in 3 non-operatively managed athletes and none managed operatively. Athletes with intrasubstance tears returned to sport at a mean of 5.6 weeks compared with 15.4 weeks for avulsions; return timing was not compared by management type.
paper.limitations: The authors could not run statistical analyses because outcomes were heterogeneous and inconsistently reported, and, because of the small number of studies, they included athletes with less than 2 years of follow-up. The sample is small and mostly male, and the title's 'prevalence' is a count of 27 published cases, not a rate in any athlete population, so it cannot show how common the injury is. D.M.K. reports grant support from Arthrex and education payments from Medwest and Smith & Nephew.
paper.practicalImplications: Isolated popliteus injury should be considered in athletes with posterolateral knee pain and effusion after forced external tibial rotation, particularly when ligamentous examination is stable. Management should be individualised because the review found no definitive algorithm, and athletes can be told that reported return to sport was about 11 weeks, with intrasubstance tears returning sooner than avulsions.
paper.athleteDev: The review addresses diagnosis, management and return to sport after a knee injury, not performance, and it reports no performance outcomes. Its only performance-relevant point is the reported return-to-sport timeline.
paper.rtp: The 13 athletes whose return was reported all returned to sport at a mean of 10.8 weeks, with intrasubstance tears returning at 5.6 weeks and avulsions at 15.4 weeks. The review has no standard return criteria, and the short and inconsistent follow-up means these timings can be used as context, not as a rule.

records.sourceFile: Preventing exertional heat stroke in football - Time for a paradigm shift.pdf

paper.citation: Anderson SA, Eichner ER, Bennett S, Boden BP, Elkins GA, Judge LW, et al. Preventing Exertional Heat Stroke in Football: Time for a Paradigm Shift. Sports Health. 2024.
paper.abstract: Clinical review of exertional heat stroke (EHS) in football, using case series from the National Registry of Catastrophic Sports Injuries and a PubMed search. It argues that prevention should focus on position-specific conditioning, linemen, heat load, and eliminating punitive exertion, rather than on uniform, hydration and acclimatization rules alone.
paper.tldr: Football heat stroke deaths in the registry cluster in linemen during conditioning, and the authors argue that prevention should shift to position-specific, intensity-limited training. The recommendations are expert opinion built on case series and have not been tested as interventions.
paper.methods: Case series of youth, high school and collegiate football deaths were drawn from the National Registry of Catastrophic Sports Injuries (1955 to 2021), whose sources are media reports, newspaper clippings, autopsy reports, death certificates, school investigations and published literature. Articles were identified through a PubMed search using the terms football, exertional heat stroke and prevention, with no screening counts or appraisal reported. The paper is a Level 5 clinical review and its recommendations are expert opinion drawn from this material.
paper.findings: Citing earlier registry analyses, the authors report that 97% of football EHS deaths from 1998 to 2018 were linemen, that 100% of high school and college deaths in a retrospective study occurred during conditioning drills and none in games, and that 37% of recent deaths involved exercise as punishment. Of deaths from 1998 to 2018, 70% occurred in shorts and a T-shirt, and the environment in recent deaths averaged a maximum of 90.8 F (32.7 C) with a wet-bulb globe temperature of 76.7 F (24.8 C). The registry shows a mean of 2 deaths per season from 1955 to 2021, rising to nearly 3 per season from 2000 to 2021, with 9 deaths in summer 2021.
paper.limitations: Registry cases are drawn largely from media and school sources, the paper has no denominator of exposed athletes, the key percentages are cited from earlier analyses rather than re-derived here, and the positional movement data in Table 1 come from 12 regular-season college games (adapted from another study) rather than from heat stroke cases. Jon K. Davis, listed in the full author section, is an employee of the Gatorade Sports Science Institute (PepsiCo) and holds PepsiCo stock options, and another listed author sits on a medical advisory board for BOA; the paper argues that dehydration contributes little to fatal EHS, and the authors state the views are not PepsiCo's.
paper.practicalImplications: Football staff should check that linemen's conditioning is position-specific and that sustained high-intensity sprints, timed conditioning tests and punitive exercise are removed, particularly in the first 7 to 10 days of a conditioning cycle. The authors also suggest adjusting activity to the heat load and considering air-conditioned spaces for linemen during hot practices, but these are expert recommendations rather than tested interventions.
paper.athleteDev: The paper argues that linemen's conditioning should match their game demands, which are short efforts at low work-to-rest ratios, and it uses positional movement data from 12 college games to support this. It reports no performance outcomes, so the training recommendations are not tested for performance effects.
paper.rtp: The paper does not address clearance after heat illness or return to sport after injury. Its one relevant point is that transition periods, including return to activity after injury, are high risk for heat stroke, so exercise intensity should be built up with appropriate work-to-rest ratios.

records.sourceFile: Prevention of concussion and long-term effects of repetitive traumatic brain injury - Unanimous consensus from the Cantu Concussion Summit.pdf

paper.citation: Cantu RC, Sills AK, Alosco ML, Arbogast KB, Bazarian JJ, Bieniek KF, et al. Prevention of concussion and long-term effects of repetitive traumatic brain injury: Unanimous consensus from the Cantu Concussion Summit. PM&R. 2025;1-4.
paper.abstract: A December 2023 summit convened clinicians and researchers to share findings and identify research gaps on brain injury and long-term cognitive disorders in athletes. After participants' advance statements and a conference discussion, the group reached unanimous agreement on six consensus statements aimed at player safety and health. The summit was supported by an unrestricted NFL educational grant.
paper.tldr: An expert summit reached unanimous agreement on six statements that call for limiting avoidable head impacts in practices and games, safer contact technique, and further research on CTE signs and TES criteria. The statements are expert consensus, not tested interventions.
paper.methods: No formal consensus method is reported beyond participants submitting three mitigation ideas in advance, aggregation of those ideas, multidisciplinary conference sessions, and a final discussion. The text does not describe how the statements were voted on or weighted.
paper.findings: The six statements are: eliminate intentional and avoidable head impacts in practices and games; limit the number, duration and intensity of head impacts; reinforce safer techniques to avoid head contact at all levels of play; penalize intentional and avoidable contact to the head and neck; investigate clinical signs and symptoms associated with CTE neuropathology; and improve TES criteria through research. The paper reports no effect data for any statement.
paper.limitations: The statements are expert opinion with no reported evidence grading or outcome data, and the head-impact limits are not quantified. The summit received an unrestricted NFL educational grant, and several authors report NFL-related roles or payments in the disclosures.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can use the statements as a policy framework for reducing avoidable head contact in practices and games and for reinforcing safer technique. The CTE and TES statements are research priorities, not clinical criteria staff can apply.
paper.athleteDev: The statements bear on practice design, particularly limiting the number, duration and intensity of head impacts in practice. The paper gives no thresholds for these limits and no performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: The paper does not address concussion diagnosis, recovery or return-to-play decisions, so it cannot guide return to sport.

records.sourceFile: Previous foot injuries associated with a greater likelihood of Achilles tendon ruptures in professional American football players.pdf

paper.citation: Krill MK, Hoffman J, Yang J, Hodax JD, Owens BD, Hewett TE. Previous foot injuries associated with a greater likelihood of Achilles tendon ruptures in professional American football players. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2018;46(3):342-348.
paper.abstract: A retrospective review of NFL injury records from 2010-11 to 2016-17 identified 109 Achilles tendon ruptures. Injury rates in the season before rupture were compared with the NFL cohort, and only foot injuries were higher in the rupture group.
paper.tldr: NFL players who ruptured an Achilles tendon had prior-season injury rates similar to the league overall and for lower-extremity injuries, but a higher foot injury rate. The foot finding rests on 6 injuries and should be treated as a hypothesis to test prospectively.
paper.methods: Retrospective online review of team injury reports, media and video for NFL seasons 2010-11 to 2016-17, with ruptures confirmed from public reports and player participation records. Injury was defined as a missed game, and injury rates per 1000 athlete-exposures (games) were compared with the NFL cohort using rate ratios with 95% CIs.
paper.findings: Among 31 analyzed players (35 game injuries in the prior season), the overall injury rate was 36.57 per 1000 AE versus 38.83 for the NFL cohort (IRR 0.94, 95% CI 0.68-1.31, p = 0.73). Lower-extremity injury IRR was 1.10 (0.76-1.58), while foot injury IRR was 2.58 (1.16-5.77, p = 0.02), with 6 foot injuries in the rupture group. Eleven players had two ruptures, and all 11 second ruptures were contralateral. The authors report more identified ruptures than the 31 reported for 1997-2002, but they give no denominator for the earlier period.
paper.limitations: Injury reports list only body part and vary in detail, and the authors' post hoc power analysis indicates the sample may be too small for body-part findings with few injuries. The text and tables disagree in places: the text gives 4228 NFL-cohort injuries while Table 2 gives 6002, the overall IRR is 0.96 (p = 0.79) in one results paragraph but 0.94 (p = 0.73) in the abstract and Table 2, and the knee count is 8 in the abstract but 9 in Table 1 and the text; table values are reported here.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff could note a prior foot injury as a possible risk marker to check in their own injury data. The paper does not show that foot injury predicts rupture, so it does not support a screening threshold or a change in clearance decisions.
paper.athleteDev: The paper measures injury rates only and reports no performance outcomes. Its discussion mentions reduced performance after rupture, but this is drawn from prior NFL work and is not measured here.
paper.rtp: The paper does not study rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes, so it cannot guide return-to-sport decisions. The discussion cites low return-to-play rates after Achilles rupture from prior work, which this study does not test.

records.sourceFile: Primary and secondary risk factors associated with concussion symptom clusters in collegiate athletes - Results from the NCAA-DoD Grand Alliance CARE Consortium.pdf

paper.citation: Nolan KE, Caccese JB, Kontos AP, Buckley TA, Garcia GP, Port N, et al. Primary and secondary risk factors associated with concussion symptom clusters in collegiate athletes: results from the NCAA-DoD Grand Alliance CARE Consortium. The Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2022;11(4):23259671231163581.
paper.abstract: A cross-sectional study of 1104 concussed collegiate athletes and service academy cadets from the CARE Consortium. Exploratory factor analysis of SCAT-3 symptoms collected 24 to 48 hours after injury identified four symptom clusters, and regression linked several pre- and post-injury factors to scores within those clusters.
paper.tldr: Concussion symptoms 24 to 48 hours after injury grouped into four clusters, with female sex, delayed reporting, less sleep and practice or training injuries linked to higher scores across clusters. Migraine history, amnesia and depression were linked to specific clusters.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional analysis of CARE Consortium participants with a concussion and a 24 to 48 hour SCAT-3 assessment, with exclusions for missing data, recent concussion and other conditions. Exploratory factor analysis (varimax rotation) defined the clusters, and generalized linear models with cluster sum scores as outcomes tested primary and secondary risk factors, with false discovery rate control.
paper.findings: The 4 clusters were cognitive fatigue, migrainous, vestibular-cognitive and affective, explaining 62% of symptom variance. Female sex was associated with higher scores in all 4 clusters (b 1.17 to 2.43), less sleep in all 4 (b -0.24 to -0.39), and delayed reporting in all 4 (b 0.97 to 1.86). Migraine history was linked to migrainous (b 1.19) and affective (b 1.07) scores, amnesia to vestibular-cognitive (b 1.18) and migrainous (b 1.47) scores, and depression to vestibular-cognitive (b 0.12) and affective (b 0.10) scores.
paper.limitations: The design is cross-sectional, so the direction of associations is unclear, and the regression models had low explanatory power (R2 0.07 to 0.12, Table 3). Of 3322 concussions initially available, 2218 were excluded; the authors cite 682 for missing data and 966 for exclusion criteria, but the exclusion counts listed in the methods sum to 1536. The sample is limited to collegiate athletes and service academy cadets, with football the largest sport, and the depression and migraine effects are small with confidence intervals near zero.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff could use the finding that delayed reporting and low sleep are linked to higher symptom scores to stress prompt reporting and sleep assessment. Migraine history and amnesia may help clinicians anticipate specific symptom patterns, but the paper does not test whether tailoring treatment to these clusters improves outcomes.
paper.athleteDev: The paper does not measure performance outcomes. Its relevance to training is limited to the finding that practice or training injuries were linked to higher symptom scores than game injuries, which may bear on how practice injuries are reported and managed.
paper.rtp: The paper does not study return-to-play decisions or recovery timelines, so it cannot guide return to sport. Symptom clusters at 24 to 48 hours are not shown to predict recovery time or readiness to return.

records.sourceFile: Protection Before Impact- the                        Potential Neuroprotective Role of Nutritional         Supplementation    in             Sports-Related Head Trauma.pdf

paper.citation: Oliver JM, Anzalone AJ, Turner SM. Protection Before Impact: the Potential Neuroprotective Role of Nutritional Supplementation in Sports-Related Head Trauma. Sports Med. 2018;48(Suppl 1):S39-S52.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of whether nutritional supplements given before head impacts (creatine, curcumin, omega-3 DHA, and their combination) could limit damage from concussive and sub-concussive impacts. Most supporting data come from rodent injury models, and the authors conclude that human trials are needed and that supplementation is not yet widely accepted or recommended.
paper.tldr: Creatine, curcumin and omega-3s reduced brain injury markers in rodent models when given before injury, but no human trial shows that taking them before head impacts protects athletes. The authors call for large clinical trials and do not recommend supplementation at present.
paper.methods: Narrative review, published in a supplement sponsored by the Gatorade Sports Science Institute. It summarizes concussion pathophysiology, then reviews animal and limited human studies of creatine, curcumin and omega-3 DHA given before injury, including their combination. No systematic search method is described.
paper.findings: In rodent controlled cortical impact models, creatine given before injury was associated with cortical tissue sparing and reduced lactate, free fatty acid and reactive oxygen accumulation, and curcumin and DHA given before injury reduced oxidative damage and axonal injury markers and improved maze performance. In humans, a single 20 g creatine dose raised brain creatine, while a 7-day study in 10-12-year-olds found no change. The authors' own study in American football athletes found lower serum neurofilament light with DHA irrespective of dose, with the low-dose group showing the greatest attenuation, though group sizes were small.
paper.limitations: The review has no described search strategy, so it cannot be checked for completeness or bias in study selection. Most evidence is rodent-based, with different injury models, doses and timings, and the authors note the gap between laboratory impacts and sports impacts. The human DHA study used small treatment groups, and its biomarker result was not tied to clinical concussion outcomes.
paper.practicalImplications: The review does not recommend supplements for concussion protection at present, and the authors call for human trials. Staff discussing creatine can use the review's safety point (no persuasive evidence of cramping, dehydration or renal harm at up to 0.8 g/kg/day for up to 5 years in the cited consensus), which is a safety statement and not evidence of head protection.
paper.athleteDev: The review does not measure performance outcomes, so it cannot justify creatine, curcumin or omega-3s as performance aids. Its creatine discussion concerns brain energy metabolism and weight gain, not athletic output.
paper.rtp: The review concerns protection before head impact and does not study recovery after concussion or return-to-play decisions. It cannot be used to shorten recovery, guide clearance, or treat a concussion with supplements.

records.sourceFile: Pseudo-Sciatica Pain Due to a Biceps Femoris Muscle Tear.pdf

paper.citation: Correia R, Correia G, Meixedo S, Correia MC, Carvalho JL. Pseudo-Sciatica Pain Due to a Biceps Femoris Muscle Tear. Cureus. 2024;16(11):e74286.
paper.abstract: Describes a 36-year-old male with sciatica-like symptoms after an acute hamstring tear during an amateur football match. Ultrasound showed a partial myotendinous rupture of the biceps femoris long head adjacent to the sciatic nerve. A structured five-week rehabilitation program was followed by reduced pain, improved strength and flexibility, according to the authors.
paper.tldr: In one amateur player, a partial biceps femoris tear lying over the sciatic nerve produced sciatica-like pain, and a five-week rehabilitation program was followed by resolution of that pain. This single case cannot establish the mechanism or the treatment effect.
paper.methods: Single-patient case report from a rehabilitation center. Assessment included history, physical examination (straight leg raise, slump test, strength, reflexes and sensation) and ultrasound before and after treatment. Treatment was 15 sessions over five weeks in three phases, covering pain and range of motion, strengthening and aerobic work, then flexibility using Askling's L-protocol. No MRI, nerve conduction study or EMG was performed.
paper.findings: Baseline ultrasound showed an immature proximal myotendinous rupture of the biceps femoris long head, about 25% of the cross-section, lying over the sciatic nerve. Straight leg raise was negative (pain only beyond 60 degrees), strength, sensation and reflexes were intact, and the slump test was described as uncertain in the case section but as producing pain and mild plantar tingling in the discussion. After rehabilitation the patient reported no sciatica pain and better gait, with pain only at the end of a squat, reduced muscle wasting, a negative resisted flexion test and healing signs on ultrasound; no numerical strength or range-of-motion values are reported.
paper.limitations: This is one patient, and the outcome is descriptive, so the abstract's claim of enhanced muscle strength cannot be checked. No electrophysiology or MRI was done, so sciatic nerve compression (attributed to inflammation or a possible hematoma) is inferred. The patient presented about two months (eight weeks) after injury; sciatica onset is given as 'two weeks' after injury in the abstract and discussion but 'after a few weeks' in the case, the slump test is reported as uncertain in one section and suggestive in another, and the rupture is 25% of the cross-section in the text but under 25% in the figure legend, with different ultrasound systems used before and after.
paper.practicalImplications: When a hamstring tear is accompanied by sciatica-like pain, this case shows that ultrasound can locate the tear relative to the sciatic nerve while neurological exam findings stay largely normal. Nerve involvement was not confirmed electrophysiologically, and the paper does not show that early rehabilitation prevents hamstring syndrome, so the case supports considering this differential rather than a specific treatment.
paper.athleteDev: The case concerns diagnosis and rehabilitation after injury, not performance. It reports no training load, strength, sprint or kicking outcomes that would inform performance programming.
paper.rtp: The patient improved in gait, squatting and flexibility, but the paper reports no return-to-play date or sport-specific test. It cannot guide return-to-play decisions for hamstring injuries with or without sciatica-like symptoms.

records.sourceFile: Psychological interventions used to                                reduce sports injuries- a systematic review  of           realworld                    effectiveness.pdf

paper.citation: Gledhill A, Forsdyke D, Murray E. Psychological interventions used to reduce sports injuries: a systematic review of real-world effectiveness. Br J Sports Med. 2018 (published online 20 February 2018).
paper.abstract: Mixed-methods systematic review of 13 papers (14 studies, 1,380 athletes) on psychological interventions for sports injury prevention in real-world settings. Thirteen of 14 studies reported fewer injuries or shorter time loss, with effect sizes from d = 0.2 to 1.21. Average risk of bias was moderate (MMAT 51.9%), and stress management was the most common approach.
paper.tldr: Stress management and multi-component psychological programs were followed by fewer injuries or less time loss in 13 of 14 studies in athletes. Small samples, moderate average risk of bias and rarely reported adherence mean these effect sizes should be treated as provisional.
paper.methods: Mixed-methods systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42016035879) reported under PRISMA. Seven databases were searched to February 2017, with hand-searching of sport psychology journals and forward and backward citation searching. Included designs were RCTs, controlled non-randomized, before-and-after and qualitative studies that delivered a specified psychological intervention to players and reported injury outcomes; three reviewers screened and appraised studies with the MMAT and synthesized by best-evidence synthesis.
paper.findings: Of the 14 studies, 13 reported fewer injuries and/or shorter time loss, with effect sizes from d = 0.2 to 1.21, and 12 had a control group. Stress inoculation training had moderate risk of bias (mean 50%) across five studies, relaxation had high risk of bias (mean 8.3%) across three studies, and multipurpose programs had low risk of bias (mean 75%) across three studies, all reporting benefit. Programs lasted 4 weeks to 8 months (mean 15.6 weeks) with 6 to 160 sessions, and compliance was reported in one study only (82% and 83%).
paper.limitations: No pooled effect size was calculated, and the authors note most studies were small with few sample-size estimates. Risk of bias was driven by unclear randomization, allocation concealment and blinding (8 studies), and female athletes were under-represented. Injury definitions ranged from none to varying time-loss definitions, the search terms were strict, and grey literature and non-English reports were excluded, while the authors note that publication bias tends to favor statistically significant studies.
paper.practicalImplications: Stress management and multi-component programs were reported as beneficial, and studies at low risk of bias found stress inoculation-based programs of up to two sessions a week for 3 to 6 weeks effective (d = 0.2 to 0.99), so staff can consider them within an injury-prevention plan. Because adherence was rarely reported and average quality was moderate, the dose athletes actually received is unclear; the authors recommend building a strong alliance with athletes and referring to qualified sport psychology professionals.
paper.athleteDev: The review measures injury rates and time loss, not performance outcomes, so it does not show that psychological training improves performance. Its positive injury findings do not establish performance benefit.
paper.rtp: The review concerns injury prevention and does not study injured athletes, so it cannot guide return-to-play or psychological readiness decisions after injury.

records.sourceFile: Public interest in America on cardiac arrest following cardiovascular events of Bronny and Damar - A Google trend study.pdf

paper.citation: Kahlam J, Sacher A, Reilly JP, Lo DF. Public interest in America on cardiac arrest following cardiovascular events of Bronny and Damar: a Google trend study. Journal Pre-proof (Elsevier, article AHJO 100433). 2024.
paper.abstract: This retrospective Google Trends study compared public search interest in six cardiac-arrest terms around the cardiac arrests of Damar Hamlin and LeBron James Jr. with a 12-month baseline. Search interest for CPR and AED was higher around Hamlin's event than James Jr.'s, and all six terms were higher in the period after Hamlin's arrest than before.
paper.tldr: Public search interest in CPR and AED rose more around Damar Hamlin's cardiac arrest than around LeBron James Jr.'s, and interest in all six terms stayed higher for months after Hamlin's arrest. The authors suggest this attention could be used for CPR education, but the study measures searches, not training or CPR use.
paper.methods: Weekly Google Trends relative search volume was extracted for six terms (cardiac arrest, CPR, basic life support, myocardial infarction, defibrillation, AED) from 8/21/2022 to 8/14/2023. Three-week windows (the event week plus two weeks) were compared with the 12-month average using one-way ANOVA and independent-sample t-tests, and a long-term comparison used 17 weeks before and 34 weeks after Hamlin's arrest, excluding the James Jr. window. Analysis used SPSS.
paper.findings: Around Hamlin's arrest, RSV was higher than around James Jr.'s for CPR (54.7 vs 22.0, P = 0.034) and AED (51.3 vs 19.3, P = 0.038), while basic life support was higher around James Jr.'s (94.3 vs 87, P = 0.031). Against the 12-month average (Table 3), only myocardial infarction around Hamlin's arrest (76.7 vs 46.6, P = 0.00 as printed) and basic life support around James Jr.'s (94.3 vs 80.9, P = 0.00 as printed) were significantly higher; cardiac arrest, CPR, defibrillation and AED around Hamlin's arrest were not (P = 0.269, 0.304, 0.271 and 0.322). Over the long term, all six terms were higher in the 34 weeks after Hamlin's arrest than in the 17 weeks before, for example CPR 18.59 to 23.56 (P < 0.00 as printed) and cardiac arrest 3.82 to 4.47 (P = 0.034).
paper.limitations: The Abstract states significant increases against baseline for cardiac arrest, CPR, defibrillation and AED around Hamlin's arrest and a P = 0.026 MI increase around James Jr.'s, but Table 3 gives non-significant P values for all of these (MI around James Jr.'s P = 0.251); the Abstract's CPR and AED comparison values (23.56 vs 22.0; 19.59 vs 19.4) are not the Table 3 event-window means, and the Results text reverses the BLS comparison ('from 94.3 to 80.9', P = 0.04) and gives defibrillation P = 0.944 where Table 3 gives 0.271. The long-term comparison has no control series, unequal window lengths and no trend adjustment, weekly values are treated as independent samples, and multiple comparisons are not addressed. The authors state it is unclear whether these searches led to more CPR education, and the study does not measure training or bystander CPR.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest the sustained rise in interest after Hamlin's arrest could be used to promote bystander CPR training, and they propose studies of CPR course enrolment and bystander CPR rates. The rise in myocardial infarction searches around Hamlin's arrest is read by the authors as possible confusion between MI and cardiac arrest, which they suggest education should address.
paper.athleteDev: Not a performance study. It examines public search interest around two athletes' cardiac arrests and does not measure training, performance or athlete outcomes.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The study does not assess medical clearance, return-to-play decisions or any individual athlete's recovery.

paper.citation: Jacobs HR, Haight MA, Nguyen A, Sajjadi NB, Hartwell M. Public interest in cardiac arrest in the United States following Damar Hamlin's injury on Monday Night Football. Resuscitation. 2023.
paper.abstract: This research letter used Google Trends to measure United States search interest in cardiac arrest, cardiopulmonary resuscitation and commotio cordis around Damar Hamlin's cardiac arrest in January 2023. An ARIMA model estimated the interest expected without the event, and actual search interest exceeded that forecast for all three terms.
paper.tldr: Search interest in cardiac arrest, CPR and commotio cordis rose sharply after Damar Hamlin's collapse and peaked on January 4, 2023. The authors suggest this public attention could be used to promote CPR and AED training.
paper.methods: Daily Google Trends relative search interest for three terms was extracted for October 12, 2022 to January 8, 2023 in the United States. An ARIMA model was constructed to forecast each term's interest had the injury not occurred, and actual and forecast values were compared. The study was judged non-human subjects research and followed STROBE guidelines.
paper.findings: The difference between actual and forecast RSI for 'cardiac arrest' was 99.01, which the authors describe as a 10,023.46% increase above the expected value. Similar differences were reported for 'cardiopulmonary resuscitation' and 'commotio cordis', with no absolute values given in the text. Peak RSI for all three terms occurred on January 4, 2023.
paper.limitations: This is a two-page uncorrected-proof research letter covering about 5 days after the event. The authors state that interest 'significantly increased' but report no statistical test, forecast values for the other two terms, model fit or confidence intervals, and the percentage increase is computed against a model-based expected value. Google Trends gives a 0-100 relative index, not absolute search volume, and the study does not measure CPR or AED training.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest that the spike in public interest could be used to sustain CPR and AED training in communities. They frame training as a life skill that could better prepare communities for emergencies, but the study does not test whether any training followed.
paper.athleteDev: Not a performance study. It measures public search interest after an athlete's cardiac arrest and does not assess athlete training or performance.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The study does not assess medical clearance, return-to-play decisions or any individual athlete's recovery.

records.sourceFile: Public online interest in injuries sustained by NFL quarterbacks.pdf

paper.citation: Torgerson T, Checketts J, Thompson J, Hanson C, Vassar M. Public Online Interest in Injuries Sustained by National Football League Quarterbacks. Arthroscopy, Sports Medicine, and Rehabilitation. 2020:e1-e8.
paper.abstract: This study used Google Trends to measure public interest in injuries to six starting NFL quarterbacks in the 2019 season, comparing observed search volume with an ARIMA forecast. Injury-related search terms were above expected for all six players, by 64% to 100%.
paper.tldr: Google searches for injury terms rose 64% to 100% above forecast after injuries to six starting NFL quarterbacks, mostly on the day after the injury. The authors suggest sports medicine clinicians could use this window for public education.
paper.methods: Starting NFL quarterbacks for 2019-2020 were identified from ESPN depth charts, and injuries were taken from the NFL injury report, with an injury defined as missing one full game. Three to five search terms per player were chosen by the authors and searched in Google Trends for July 22 to October 22, 2019 (Mahomes: September 1 to December 1, 2019). Observed relative search volume was compared with an ARIMA forecast built from the pre-injury period, using R and Stata.
paper.findings: The day after each injury, all injury-related terms were above expected, ranging from 63.9% (Roethlisberger 'elbow surgery') to 100% (Roethlisberger 'what happened to' and Brees 'recovery') (Table 1). Newton's and Darnold's announcements produced their highest search volumes on the day of the announcement rather than the day after. Several terms stayed above expected the following week, for example Brees 'recovery' and 'gamekeeper's thumb' by 22% to 44%, and Darnold 'mono' by 27% (95% CI 4 to 50).
paper.limitations: The study covers Google only and does not measure social media, and it cannot show whether searchers wanted education or simply news. Newton and Darnold were not game injuries, and the abstract's 'all 6 injured quarterbacks' and 'first 3 days' wording goes beyond the day-after and following-week results, which report no day-by-day analysis for days 1 to 3. The search windows differ between players, the search terms were chosen by the authors, the Google Trends values are relative, and the ARIMA model details are not reported. Table 1 gives no value for 'what happened to' Cam Newton or Sam Darnold because search peaks came before their announcements, and the 'significant increases' wording is not backed by reported tests beyond the 95% confidence intervals.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors recommend that orthopaedic and sports medicine clinicians use social media within about 3 days of a televised injury to share informed opinions, and that journals prepare editorials on common injuries in advance. These recommendations are the authors' opinion and were not tested; the study shows public search interest, not whether such posts reach or help patients.
paper.athleteDev: Not a performance study. It measures public search interest after NFL quarterback injuries and does not assess athlete performance, training or outcomes.
paper.rtp: Limited return-to-sport relevance. The study does not measure recovery times, return-to-play decisions or clinical outcomes, and its 'recovery' search terms reflect public interest rather than recovery data.
